title: Water demand estimation
summary: Duty and delta are the two quantities everything is expressed in, and they are inversely related — a higher duty means more land irrigated per cumec, which is better. The relation delta = 8.64B/D converts between them and is worth memorising in that exact form. The other reliable marks are the soil moisture constants (field capacity, wilting point, available moisture) and the efficiency chain, whose components MULTIPLY, which is why traditional surface irrigation manages only 35 to 45 percent overall.

sections.heading: Crop water requirement
sections.body:
**Consumptive use (evapotranspiration)** is the water actually used by the crop:

> **Consumptive use = Evaporation (from soil and water surfaces) + Transpiration (through the plant)**

The crop's requirement then follows:

> **Crop water requirement CWR = ET_crop − effective rainfall**
> **ET_crop = K_c × ET₀**

where **ET₀** is the **reference (potential) evapotranspiration** — the demand of the atmosphere on a standard reference surface — and **K_c** the **crop coefficient**.

**The crop coefficient varies through the growing season**, which is the part candidates overlook:

| Growth stage | K_c |
|---|---|
| **Initial** (establishment, little canopy) | **0.3 – 0.5** |
| Development | rising |
| **Mid-season** (full canopy) | **1.0 – 1.2** — the peak |
| Late season (maturity, senescence) | falling to 0.3 – 0.7 |

So the water requirement is not constant: it peaks at full canopy, and the **canal must be sized for that peak**, not for the seasonal average.

**Estimating ET₀:**

| Method | Basis | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **Penman / FAO Penman–Monteith** | **Energy balance + aerodynamic term** | **The most rigorous** and the modern reference |
| **Blaney–Criddle** | Temperature and daylight hours | Simple; widely used where data is scarce |
| Hargreaves | Temperature and radiation | Simple |
| Thornthwaite | Temperature | Simple |
| Modified Penman | — | Common in Indian practice |

**Penman is the answer to "which is most rigorous"**, because it accounts for both physical requirements of evaporation: the **energy** available to change water to vapour, and the **capacity of the air** to carry the vapour away. Temperature-only methods work because temperature correlates with radiation, but they fail where **wind or humidity** is unusual — which in Nepal means they can mislead in the Terai's humid monsoon and in the dry, windy trans-Himalayan valleys alike.

**Effective rainfall** is the portion of rainfall actually available to the crop — excluding surface runoff, deep percolation below the root zone, and interception losses. It is **not** the measured rainfall. For a monsoon-fed crop in Nepal the distinction is large: a heavy monsoon storm may deliver 100 mm of which only 40 mm is effective, the rest running off or percolating away.

That is why **rice in the Nepali monsoon** needs relatively little supplementary irrigation while **wheat in the winter** needs a great deal, despite rice's far higher total water use.

**Typical water requirements (delta):**

| Crop | Delta (cm) | Base period (days) |
|---|---|---|
| **Rice (paddy)** | **100 – 125** | 120 – 150 |
| Sugarcane | 90 – 150 | 320 – 360 |
| **Wheat** | **35 – 40** | 100 – 120 |
| Maize | 45 – 50 | 100 – 110 |
| Cotton | 45 – 50 | 200 – 240 |
| Vegetables | 45 – 60 | 60 – 90 |

**Rice's very high delta** is not because the plant transpires more than others but because of **continuous ponding**: the standing water percolates and evaporates continuously. That is why **alternate wetting and drying** or the **System of Rice Intensification (SRI)** can cut rice water use substantially with no loss of yield — a genuinely important result for a country where rice dominates the irrigated area.

**Crop seasons in Nepal**, which questions reference:

| Season | Period | Principal crops |
|---|---|---|
| **Kharif (monsoon)** | June – October | **Rice**, maize, millet |
| **Rabi (winter)** | November – March | **Wheat**, barley, mustard, potato, vegetables |
| **Spring / summer** | March – June | Maize, spring rice, vegetables |

Irrigation matters most in the **rabi and spring** seasons, when rainfall is minimal — which is exactly when river flows are at their lowest. That coincidence of maximum demand with minimum supply is the central problem of Nepali irrigation, and the argument for storage.

sections.heading: Duty, delta and the base period
sections.body:
**The three quantities and their definitions:**

| Term | Definition | Units |
|---|---|---|
| **Duty (D)** | The **area irrigated per unit of continuous discharge** | **hectares per cumec** (ha/m³/s) |
| **Delta (Δ)** | The **total depth of water** applied to the crop over its base period | **centimetres** |
| **Base period (B)** | The period from the **first watering to the last** | **days** |

**The relation between them** — derived rather than memorised:

A discharge of 1 cumec running continuously for B days delivers a volume of **1 × B × 24 × 60 × 60 = 86 400 B** cubic metres. Spread over D hectares (= 10 000 D m²) this gives a depth of

> **Δ (metres) = 86 400 B / (10 000 D) = 8.64 B / D**

and since Δ is conventionally in centimetres:

> **Δ (cm) = 8.64 B / D**   with B in days and D in ha/cumec

**Duty and delta are INVERSELY related.** A crop needing a large depth of water (high delta) irrigates less land per cumec (low duty). And:

> **A HIGHER duty is BETTER** — more hectares served by each cumec of supply.

That direction is worth fixing, because it is the point of the concept: duty measures the **productivity of the water**, and improving irrigation efficiency raises it.

**Worked example.** For rice with Δ = 120 cm and B = 120 days:

> D = 8.64 × 120 / 120 = **8.64 ha/cumec**

For wheat with Δ = 40 cm and B = 120 days:

> D = 8.64 × 120 / 40 = **25.9 ha/cumec**

So one cumec irrigates **three times as much wheat as rice** — which is the quantitative basis of any argument about cropping pattern and water scarcity.

**Factors affecting duty**, all of which act by changing the losses or the demand:

| Factor | Effect on duty |
|---|---|
| **Lining the canal** | **Increases** duty (less seepage) |
| Efficient application at the field | Increases |
| **Rainfall during the base period** | Increases (less irrigation needed) |
| Soil type — sandy | **Decreases** (higher percolation) |
| **Climate** — hot, dry, windy | Decreases (higher ET) |
| Crop type | Rice low, wheat high |
| Method of irrigation — drip or sprinkler | **Increases** substantially |
| Long conveyance distance | Decreases (more transit loss) |

**Duty at different points** is a subtlety worth noting: duty measured at the **field outlet** is higher than duty at the **canal head**, because losses occur in between. A question specifying "duty at the head of the main canal" is asking for the lower figure, and the ratio between them is the conveyance efficiency.

**Kor watering and the outlet factor.** The **kor watering** is the **first watering after the plant has grown a few centimetres** — a critical irrigation, since the young crop cannot survive its absence.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Kor depth** | The **depth** of the kor watering (about 13.5 cm for both rice and wheat) |
| **Kor period** | The **duration** within which it must be completed (2–4 weeks) |

> **Outlet discharge factor = kor depth ÷ kor period**

**The canal capacity is fixed by the kor period**, because that is when the demand rate is highest — the whole area must receive its kor watering within a short window. Sizing the canal on the seasonal average demand would leave it unable to deliver the kor watering, and the crop would fail at its most vulnerable stage.

**Command areas**, which questions ask to be distinguished:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **GCA — gross command area** | The **total area** enclosed by the canal system's boundary |
| **CCA — culturable command area** | The part of the GCA that is **culturable** (excluding villages, roads, ponds, barren land) |
| **NCA — net command area** | The part actually **irrigated** |
| **Intensity of irrigation** | (area cropped in a year ÷ CCA) × 100% |

**Cropping intensity can exceed 100%** where two or three crops a year are grown on the same land — and raising it is usually the **object of irrigation investment**, since it multiplies output from the same land. An intensity of 180% means most of the land carries two crops a year.

sections.heading: Soil moisture and irrigation scheduling
sections.body:
**Soil moisture constants**, in descending order of water content:

| Constant | Definition |
|---|---|
| **Saturation** | All pores filled with water |
| **Field capacity (FC)** | Water retained **after gravity drainage** has ceased (1–3 days) |
| **Available moisture** | **FC − PWP** — the water the plant **can** extract |
| **Readily available moisture** | The fraction (about 50–75%) extracted **without stress** |
| **Permanent wilting point (PWP)** | Water content at which the plant **cannot extract** more and wilts irrecoverably |
| Hygroscopic water | Held so tightly it is unavailable to any plant |

> **Available moisture = Field capacity − Permanent wilting point**

and irrigation is normally applied when about **50%** of the available moisture has been used — before the plant experiences stress, but not so early that water is wasted and the soil is kept waterlogged.

**Typical values by soil texture:**

| Soil | Field capacity | Wilting point | Available moisture |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Sandy** | 10 – 15% | 4 – 6% | **6 – 9%** — low |
| Sandy loam | 15 – 22% | 6 – 10% | 9 – 12% |
| **Loam** | 22 – 30% | 10 – 14% | **12 – 16%** — highest |
| Clay loam | 28 – 35% | 14 – 18% | 14 – 17% |
| **Clay** | 32 – 40% | 18 – 24% | **14 – 16%** |

**Loam holds the most available moisture**, which is why it is the best agricultural soil: sand drains too fast to hold much, and clay holds a great deal but binds much of it too tightly to release. That the *available* fraction peaks at loam, while the *total* held rises monotonically with clay content, is the instructive point.

**Depth of water to apply:**

> **d = (γ_d / γ_w) × D × (FC − present moisture content)**

where γ_d is the dry unit weight of the soil, D the root zone depth, and the moisture contents by weight. Root zone depths: **shallow-rooted 30–60 cm** (vegetables, rice), **medium 60–100 cm** (wheat, maize), **deep 100–200 cm** (sugarcane, orchards).

**Frequency of irrigation:**

> **Interval (days) = readily available moisture depth / daily consumptive use rate**

So a crop using 5 mm/day on a soil holding 50 mm of readily available moisture in its root zone needs watering every **10 days** — and a sandy soil, holding less, needs **more frequent but smaller** irrigations. That is why light soils are unsuited to surface irrigation with long intervals and suit **drip** particularly well.

**Methods of irrigation:**

| Method | Application efficiency | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **Wild flooding** | **30 – 40%** | Rough land, low-value crops; wasteful |
| **Border strip** | 50 – 60% | Close-growing crops on gentle uniform slopes |
| **Check basin** | 55 – 65% | **Rice**, orchards; level basins |
| **Furrow** | 55 – 70% | **Row crops** — maize, sugarcane, vegetables, potato |
| **Sprinkler** | **70 – 80%** | Undulating land, **sandy soil**, most crops; light soils where surface methods fail |
| **Drip (trickle)** | **85 – 95%** | **Row crops, orchards, vegetables**; scarce or saline water; steep or sandy land |
| Subsurface | 80 – 90% | Special cases |

**Drip irrigation's advantages** are worth listing because they go beyond efficiency: water is delivered **directly to the root zone** so evaporation and percolation losses nearly vanish; the soil between rows stays dry so **weed growth falls**; **fertiliser can be applied through the system** (fertigation) with high uptake; and **saline water can be used** at a lower salinity hazard, because the soil is kept continuously moist rather than cycling between wet and dry.

Against which: **high capital cost**, **clogging of emitters** (requiring filtration and periodic acid treatment), damage by rodents, and the need for a **pressurised supply**. In Nepal, drip has been adopted successfully for **high-value vegetables and orchards** in the hills, where water is scarce, land is steep and the crop justifies the investment — and much less for cereals, where the economics do not work.

**Land levelling** deserves a note, because it is the cheapest efficiency improvement available for surface irrigation. An unlevelled field is irrigated by over-applying until the highest point is wetted, which means the low points are grossly over-irrigated. Proper levelling can raise application efficiency from 40% to 60% at modest cost — a better return than any change of method.

sections.heading: Irrigation efficiencies and water management
sections.body:
**The efficiency chain — and the crucial property is that the components MULTIPLY:**

| Efficiency | Definition | Typical |
|---|---|---|
| **Conveyance efficiency η_c** | Water delivered to the field ÷ water diverted at the head | **60 – 80% unlined**, **85 – 95% lined** |
| **Application (field) efficiency η_a** | Water stored in the root zone ÷ water delivered to the field | **40 – 70% surface**, 75% sprinkler, 90% drip |
| **Use (storage) efficiency η_s** | Water stored ÷ water needed | 70 – 90% |
| **Distribution efficiency η_d** | Uniformity of application across the field | 70 – 90% |
| **Overall (project) efficiency** | **The PRODUCT of the components** | **30 – 50%** typical surface system |

> **η_overall = η_c × η_a × η_s × …**

**The multiplication is why traditional surface irrigation manages only 35–45% overall**, and it is the most useful insight in the subchapter. Even respectable-looking component figures compound badly: 75% conveyance × 60% application = **45%**, before any other loss. It follows that **improving the worst component gives the greatest return** — and in most systems the worst is either an unlined canal or an unlevelled field.

It also follows that a system quoted as "80% efficient" without specifying **which** efficiency is being claimed is meaningless. A question giving component efficiencies and asking for the overall value is testing exactly this.

**Where the water goes** in a surface system delivering 100 units at the canal head:

| Loss | Typical share |
|---|---|
| **Seepage from the canal** | 15 – 30 |
| **Evaporation from the canal** | 1 – 3 |
| **Deep percolation below the root zone** | 10 – 25 |
| **Surface runoff (tail water)** from the field | 5 – 15 |
| **Stored usefully in the root zone** | **35 – 50** |

**Not all "losses" are truly lost**, and this is a distinction worth making: **seepage and deep percolation recharge the groundwater**, which may then be pumped and used. In a closed basin with conjunctive use, therefore, basin-scale efficiency is much higher than field-scale efficiency suggests. **Evaporation and flows to a saline sink are the genuine losses**; percolation to a usable aquifer is a **delay and a cost**, not a destruction.

That is why modern water management distinguishes **consumed** water (evaporated and transpired, genuinely gone) from **non-consumed** water (returned to the system, recoverable) — and why lining every canal is not always the best investment.

**Improving efficiency**, in rough order of cost-effectiveness:

| Measure | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Land levelling** | Raises application efficiency substantially at modest cost |
| **Canal lining** in high-seepage reaches | Raises conveyance efficiency; target the worst reaches, not the whole length |
| **Proper scheduling** (irrigate on soil moisture, not by habit) | Avoids over-application |
| **Rotational water supply (warabandi)** | Fair, predictable distribution; reduces over-irrigation by head-enders |
| **Water user associations** and volumetric charging | Aligns incentives |
| **Piped distribution** in place of open channels | Eliminates seepage and evaporation |
| Sprinkler or drip conversion | Large gain, high capital cost |
| **Conjunctive use** of surface and groundwater | Uses the percolated water; lowers the water table |

**Water distribution systems:**

| System | Character |
|---|---|
| **Continuous flow** | Water flows constantly; simple, but suits only large holdings and abundant supply |
| **Rotational (warabandi)** | Each farmer receives the **full channel discharge for a fixed time** on a fixed roster |
| **Demand-based** | Water supplied on request; needs measurement and control |

**Warabandi is the system that works with scarce water and small holdings**, and its logic is instructive: rather than giving everyone a small trickle continuously — which is hard to control, easy to steal and inefficient to apply — it gives each farmer the **whole flow for a short, guaranteed period**. That makes the delivery **large enough to irrigate efficiently**, **verifiable** (so theft is visible), and **equitable** (the roster is public and fixed). Its weakness is inflexibility: the turn comes whether or not the crop needs water that week.

**Nepal's irrigation context** deserves the closing note, because it is distinctive:

| Feature | Significance |
|---|---|
| **Farmer-managed irrigation systems (FMIS)** | A **large share of Nepal's irrigated area** is managed by farmers themselves, some for centuries — with their own water allocation rules, maintenance labour obligations and dispute resolution |
| Small, fragmented holdings | Limits mechanisation and capital-intensive methods |
| **Monsoon-dominated flow** | Maximum demand (rabi, spring) coincides with **minimum supply** |
| Steep terrain in the hills | Small run-of-river diversions, short canals, high seepage on unstable slopes |
| Terai groundwater | Shallow tubewells give **flexible, on-demand** supply — the fastest-growing irrigation source |

**Farmer-managed systems perform surprisingly well** — often better per unit of investment than agency-managed schemes — because the users bear the consequences of poor maintenance directly and hold the local knowledge. That finding has shaped Nepali policy toward **participatory irrigation management** and the **transfer of agency systems to water user associations**, and it is worth knowing as more than a policy fact: it reflects the general engineering truth that a system's sustainability depends on who maintains it, not only on how well it was designed.

formulas.label: Duty and delta relation
formulas.expression: Δ (cm) = 8.64 B / D     (B in days, D in ha/cumec)
formulas.note: Duty and delta are INVERSELY related. A higher duty is better — more land per cumec.

formulas.label: Crop water requirement
formulas.expression: CWR = ET_crop − effective rainfall ;   ET_crop = K_c × ET₀
formulas.note: K_c varies through the season, peaking at 1.0–1.2 at full canopy. Size the canal for the PEAK.

formulas.label: Available moisture
formulas.expression: Available moisture = Field capacity − Permanent wilting point
formulas.note: Irrigate when about 50% has been used. Loam holds the most AVAILABLE moisture.

formulas.label: Depth of irrigation water to apply
formulas.note: D is the root zone depth: 30–60 cm shallow, 60–100 medium, 100–200 deep-rooted.

formulas.label: Frequency of irrigation
formulas.expression: interval (days) = readily available moisture depth / daily consumptive use
formulas.note: Sandy soils hold less, so they need more frequent but smaller irrigations.

formulas.label: Outlet discharge factor
formulas.expression: outlet factor = kor depth / kor period
formulas.note: The canal capacity is fixed by the KOR PERIOD, when the demand rate is highest.

formulas.label: Overall irrigation efficiency
formulas.note: The components MULTIPLY — which is why traditional surface systems manage only 35–45% overall.

formulas.label: Command areas and intensity
formulas.expression: GCA ⊃ CCA ⊃ NCA ;   intensity = (annual cropped area / CCA) × 100%
formulas.note: Intensity can exceed 100% where two or three crops a year are grown — usually the object of investment.
